1:
The book's first word is technical, and Calvin spends his space there. The noun comes from a verb meaning to see, yet it is not the term Scripture uses for the symbolic sights granted when God wished an extraordinary event confirmed; another word carries those, and he traces both through Samuel and the passage distinguishing two ordinary methods of revelation. What it conveys here is certainty: nothing stands in this book that God did not make known. The derivation earns its keep, he says, showing the prophets did not speak of their own accord or draw on their imaginations, but had their eyes opened to see what they could not otherwise have understood. Ellicott takes the word as a state rather than a guarantee, more or less ecstatic, in which a man sees what others do not, the things still to come and the unseen working of eternal laws.

Behind the word stands an older one. Ellicott notes that seer was the earlier name for the man and vision the correlative for his work, and thinks the older title fell out because pretenders to that clairvoyance discredited it; the prophet did not thereby stop being a seer, and to see visions remained among the highest gifts of the Spirit. Clarke supplies two terms, the seeing person who perceives what God designs and the man who has supernatural revelations, both rendered by one English word. Wesley draws the plain inference: prophecies are called visions because they stood before the prophet's mind as clearly as objects before the eye. Henry adds that the sight came while he was awake, and men who saw could not but speak, seeing how much everyone around them was concerned.

The man himself is quickly settled and slowly disputed. Gill gives the name two senses, the Lord shall save or the salvation of the Lord, either suitable to the errand. Henry prefers the second, fitting a prophet who would speak so much of a Saviour. On the father Henry is careful: not Amos the prophet, the names differing more in Hebrew than in English, but by Jewish tradition a brother or son of a king of Judah, a tradition he calls as uncertain as the rule that produced it, which makes a prophet's father a prophet wherever he is named. Pupils and successors are often called sons, he observes, and prophets' own sons rarely succeeded them.

Clarke turns from title to office and takes a position. The verb behind prophet means not only to foretell but to pray and entreat, and the man was the general preacher of his day, foreseeing disaster and spending his time counselling sinners and interceding against the judgment he announced. From this he draws the conclusion the rest will lean on: such predictions, however positive their terms, were generally conditional, stated or implied, and a later prophet was given a key that opens the difficulty. God is master of his own ways and has made man free; those who would bind him by a doctrine of fatalism put contradictory sentiments in his messengers' mouths.

Last the scope. Henry takes the title from the substance, Judah and Jerusalem, with little on the ten tribes and only some chapters on Babylon, Egypt and Tyre, nations the Jews had dealings with. Calvin puts it more sharply: everything else may be called accidental and foreign to the subject, since a title need announce only the principal matter. Ellicott makes the two names the centre, not the limit. Wesley makes the same allowance and counts: the four reigns named let us gather the office was exercised above fifty years together. Delitzsch begins where none of the others do, with the reigns, setting the long bloom of the northern kingdom beside the southern that outlasted it, and noting the splendour held the germ of its own decay.
2:
The court opens by summoning witnesses, and they disagree who is called. Gill allows either the heavens and earth themselves or, figuratively, their inhabitants, angels and men. Calvin will not have the figure: reading angels and men weakens the words and destroys their majesty, since the point is that God turns to elements dumb and without feeling because men have lost their ears. He defends the address by noting that dumb creatures do hear God's voice, the order of nature being nothing but the obedience every part of the world renders, the sea keeping its boundary and the ground yielding fruit at his bidding. Henry takes both roads: let the lights of heaven shame their darkness and the fruitfulness of earth their barrenness, or let angels and men judge between God and his vineyard.

Everyone hears Moses behind it. Clarke sets the scene as a public pleading before the world, the prophet acting as herald calling the court to order, and gathers the parallels: the psalm where God summons mankind from east to west with a consuming fire before him, and the prophet who calls the mountains and the strong foundations of the earth to hear a controversy. Moses said the same plainly, setting life and death before them, and the poetical apostrophe throws the personification into a stronger light. Ellicott grants the words recall the song but blocks the inference some draw: the thought was the common inheritance of Hebrew poets, so the parallel settles nothing about the date of either book.

Two smaller quarrels follow. Calvin observes that almost all commentators stop the clause at the announcement that the Lord has spoken, as though every ear should open the moment God speaks; he grants the sense looks fuller and rejects it anyway, the context requiring the hearing to attach to the complaint that follows. Clarke worries about the tense, preferring the present, since it is improper to demand attention to a speech already delivered, though he lets the received reading stand. Ellicott notes where the emphasis falls: sons stands first in the Hebrew, and the indictment starts from God's fatherhood, the people unworthy of election but chosen all the same.

Then the animals. Clarke quotes Bochart to sharpen the insult: the ox and ass are about the stupidest beasts there are, yet they acknowledge an owner and know the manger, though fed for his good and not their own, counted burden-bearers rather than children and worn with daily labour; while Israel, chosen by mere favour and adopted and promoted, would not acknowledge a Lord whose commandments were in the highest degree equitable. He ranks the rival images, finding a later prophet's stork and crane elegant but with less severity. Ellicott explains why these beasts and not the horse and dog: these were that world's representative domestic animals. Delitzsch adds the philology of the crib and notes the plural for master is not numerical but amplifying, the authority over the animal.

Calvin makes the comparison a general indictment of humanity. Beasts have no reason, yet can be taught to recognise who feeds them, and a people fed not merely at a stall but daily with spiritual food deserves to be sent to school among oxen. He presses further than the verse requires: scarcely any animal is cruel to its own kind, seeing its likeness in another; beasts rear their young while mothers forget the voice of nature and forsake theirs; they take no more food than sustains their strength, while men gorge and ruin their constitutions; in a word they do not transgress the laws prescribed them. Wesley keeps the definition practical, knowing here including reverence and obedience. Delitzsch places the overture at a boundary line, the methods of divine education exhausted, nothing left but to let the nation be dissolved in fire and a new one made from the gold that survives.
4:
The opening cry is hard to name. Delitzsch denies the two similar interjections sort into oh and woe, and calls this one an exclamation of pain, a lamentation filled with wrath rather than a denunciation. Ellicott hears the opposite note, indignation rather than pity. Calvin reports that some make it grief and Jerome rendered it so, and settles for astonishment and sorrow together, since men cry out when a thing is too disgraceful for plain words or words fail the feeling. Gill offers functions rather than a tone: a call to listen, a lament over settled wickedness, or a threat.

The four titles are read as an inverted election. Delitzsch shows each epithet pointing back at what Israel was chosen to be, a holy nation become a sinning one, recording what the people made of themselves. Ellicott sees a sequence in the verbs, not a heap: men forsake, then spurn, then apostatise openly; and he pauses on the name for God used here, the one Isaiah returns to most, fourteen times in the book's first part and sixteen in the second, gathering up every idea of consecration and purity. Clarke works on the words, preferring corrupted to corrupters and estranged to gone away backward on manuscript evidence, and paraphrases: they have turned their backs on him.

Then a question turning on two letters. Clarke reads where rather than why: on what part will you be struck, no whole limb being left to strike. He supports it from the Latin and a Jewish commentator, and reaches for the poets: one says there is no room on us for a new stripe, another that a man full of miseries has nowhere to put more. He addresses the question to the instruments of vengeance, not the sufferers. Delitzsch lays both out, notes the objection that the local sense is spiritless since a struck limb can be struck again, and decides for the other, to what end. Calvin decides the same, hearing a physician declare every remedy tried and his skill exhausted. Ellicott adds that the words are a plea and not a prediction.

The body becomes the argument. Ellicott suspects the writer knew what he described: the passage is a natural parable of ethics, recalling Plato on the ulcerated souls of tyrants, but he thinks it may rest on training in the medicine of the day, notes the diseases that fell on two kings as judgments, remembers the prophet prescribing for a boil, and takes the order to have practised healing against physicians who worked by charms. Calvin refuses to read the wounds as punishments only, since the clause about dressing them would mean nothing, and makes the sore a hidden fountain sending up venom that cannot be stopped. Clarke supplies the surgery: eastern medicine is mostly external, oil its chief material, a traveller reporting oil and melted grease used in India for wounds.

Last the land, and a quarrel about when. Clarke says the desolation cannot belong to the prosperous reigns and fits Ahaz, then objects that the idolatry named later is too mild for a king who spread the grossest sort and passed his son through the fire, and places the oracle at the end of the previous reign. Ellicott takes the description as current: invasions from two directions in one reign, an Assyrian campaign in the next. Delitzsch reads the vocabulary, finding nearly every word drawn from the curses of the law, the prophet deliberately describing his own time in the terms of that threat. On the last clause Ellicott reports conjectures, an overthrow of Sodom or of a rainstorm, the noun used elsewhere only of the cities of the plain; Calvin records the same dissatisfaction, the received reading being a tautology or an identical comparison. Wesley keeps the strangers and explains their thoroughness: men who do not expect to keep a country spare nothing.
8:
The two shelters need explaining, and they explain from travel. Clarke describes a temporary hut of boughs or turf, put up against the heat by day and dews by night while the fruit ripens and pulled down after; the watch was needed against jackals, which a traveller found common at vintage and able to ruin whole vineyards and cucumber gardens. Calvin, recognising the practice from France, adds a traveller's Levant account: such beds are chiefly of cucumbers, eaten unpeeled with a glass of water after, the common people's ordinary food for three or four months, so that a child asking for something to eat is handed one raw instead of bread. Delitzsch fixes the season: both plots are pictured before harvest, when watching is necessary, and the point is that no human being is visible in either, only the hut and the night hammock to show anyone is there.

The third comparison stops them all. Ellicott admits it is startling to compare a besieged city to a besieged city, and rescues it as rhetoric: the place was not under siege, but so hemmed about and cut off from help that it came to the same thing, or stood within measurable distance of it. Delitzsch asks outright and canvasses the answers others give, a watch-tower among them. Gill and Wesley take the plainer half, the city left solitary and the villages round laid waste, and Delitzsch draws the one comfort: that anything is left shows the land was not entirely emptied.

The remnant is where the chapter turns. Delitzsch works the noun, an escaped thing, and the qualifier, a remnant that was a mere trifle, and puts the divine name first for emphasis, since but for compassion it would long ago have been all over with Israel. Calvin makes the desolation present rather than threatened and warns against flattery: they would now be what those cities are, had God not kept a seed. Gill reads the remnant through the apostle who quoted the verse, identifying it with the few who believed and escaped a doomed generation. Ellicott wonders whether the idea was pressed on the prophet by the actual remnant that escaped the Assyrian kings.

Then the address that made the chapter notorious. Clarke sees how it was produced: the cities named in passing suggested the title, and he compares the same elegant turn twice in an epistle of Paul. Ellicott notices the king is not addressed, and guesses the prophet trusted him but not his ministers; the judges he does address were probably men outwardly busy in a reformation the chronicler could praise, where Isaiah saw beneath the surface. Calvin denies the two names mark any difference of rank or guilt, rulers and people being thrown into one bundle. Henry observes that the prophet knew not how to give flattering titles, and reports the Jewish tradition that he was impeached for this long afterwards and put to death for cursing the gods and speaking evil of his people's ruler.

The sacrifices are dismissed without being condemned. Calvin has God speak in person, since a lawgiver must interpret his own law lest it be abused, and sacrifice was designed to aid piety, not constitute holiness; the Jews thought their duty done when the beasts were killed, and complained of harshness when the prophets asked more. Wesley makes it a category mistake, offerings brought to a spirit who wants the life as well as the body. Gill says they could neither expiate sin nor profit God. Clarke sets a contemporary prophet's version beside it and reaches past Scripture to a Roman satirist and to Plato for the same doctrine: sacrifice and prayer profit nobody without an upright life. Ellicott places the verse in a long line of prophetic sayings on acceptable worship, and notes the tense: not what God said once but what he will say for ever.
12:
Coming before God is a technical phrase, and Clarke finds the sentence wrongly divided. The Greek runs one verse into the next for a different sense: to tread my court you shall not add, meaning you shall not be accepted in worship again. Ellicott keeps the received text, notes the Syriac and some moderns read to see my face rather than appear before it, and observes that either way the worshippers thought themselves brought nearer by entering the courts. Gill and Wesley name the occasions, the three annual feasts. Calvin makes the question the argument: in vain does anyone offer what God has not required, since he will not be worshipped in a manner of our devising, as men would see if they remembered obedience is all that is left them.

The offerings are named, and the names are disputed. Delitzsch takes the vegetable offering as a lying one, a hypocritical dead work with nothing behind what it appears to express, and reports the Greek, Latin and Gesenius taking the next word for the daily incense of the holy place; he objects, on the ground of a psalm where a layman offers it. Ellicott notes the word is not the usual one for incense and is used elsewhere of the sweet smoke of rams, but sees no reason to shift the meal-offering from its usual sense, the prophet heaping up ritual phrases without close attention. Gill calls the oblations vain, offered in hypocrisy and leaned on for pardon.

The calendar comes next, and Clarke rewrites it. Where the received text has new moons and sabbaths, he reads the fast and the day of restraint, the Greek apparently finding a different word, arguing that the prophet could hardly have left the fast out of a list of solemnities, or out of an indictment of hypocrisy he handles at length later; a minor prophet twice joins the two in one breath. Ellicott keeps the traditional list and finds it agreeing with the Chronicler's. Delitzsch pauses over my soul, taking it as the centre of God's being pervaded by self-consciousness, so that what it hates is hated to the utmost bounds of that being.

Then prayer, and Calvin is careful where he might have been sweeping. The custom of spreading the hands came not from superstition or idle ambition but from nature prompting men to declare by an outward sign that they betake themselves to God; unable to fly to him they lift themselves so. No command was given the fathers about it, yet they used it as inspired men; idolaters are convicted by the gesture, signalling a flight to God while going to idols. Not the hands are condemned but the hypocrisy behind them. Ellicott furnishes the posture from Greek and Roman practice as well as Jewish, hands stretched skyward, and notes fixed forms are barely provided for in the law, the eighteen daily prayers belonging to a later stage.

The remedy is put in short imperatives. Delitzsch counts them, three of removal and five of practice, the first of the five laying the foundation, since doing good is a difficult art in which good intentions do not make a man proficient. Four of the five concern courts, no prophet turning so keen an eye on the state and its judicial proceedings. Henry states the principle: justice will never atone for profaneness, nor prayers for oppression, righteousness towards men being as much a branch of religion as religion is of righteousness. Ellicott corrects the translation: the call is not to relieve the oppressed but to correct the oppressor, requiring rulers to use their authority against wrongdoers of their own order; and he quotes Shakespeare on Time, whose work it is to wrong the wronger till he render right. Clarke prefers to amend what is corrupted, admitting he is not perfectly satisfied with it.
18:
What sort of tribunal is this. Ellicott warns that the English suggests a discussion between equals, where the Hebrew has the tone of an ultimatum, a judge addressing an accused with no defence or a sham one; and the ultimatum turns out to be repent and be forgiven. Delitzsch agrees it is a formal trial and adds that Israel must lose, its righteousness being sham righteousness which examination turns into its opposite. Calvin paraphrases the invitation: let us both find out which has offended the other, and if you have sinned against me I still hope to convert you. He thinks the particle carries the confidence of a good cause, and that hypocrites should be handled so, since they enter disputes with God boldly and there is no end to their reasonings. Gill locates the bar: not justice, where nobody answers one charge in a thousand, but mercy.

The colours are worked over hard. Clarke derives the first from a root meaning to double, so twice dipped, preferring that to a derivation from whetting that would make the point the sharpness of the hue; the second is properly the worm, whence our vermeil, the dye got from an insect bred on a shrub of the ilex kind, still found in Provence and Languedoc, known by an Arabic name from which crimson comes. Ellicott traces both to Tyrian dyes and suspects they gained an edge because robes of those colours were worn by the princes addressed; to the prophet's eye the darker was the stain of blood. Men might dye their souls what hue they chose, he says, but bleaching was God's work.

Then the choice, put as a play on one verb. Delitzsch sets the halves against each other, eating the good of the land or being eaten by the sword, and notes both blessing and curse were proclaimed long before, so the justified stand where the nation first stood. Clarke prefers the versions that let the sword do the devouring, an easier construction and better rhythm. Ellicott registers a disappointment rather than hiding it: temporal goods promised where one wanted the peace and joy of a penitent psalm. His answer is that the audience was unjust and selfish and nowhere near a contrite heart, so the prophet was content to wake the dormant sense of righteousness and let them learn they would not lose by changing.

Calvin turns aside twice to fight about the will. The papists, he says, argue that if men are happy whenever willing to obey, the choosing must lie in their own power. He calls the argument childish. When God charges obstinacy he is not measuring our capacity for good or evil, but telling us whose fault it is that we lack good things, and that our calamities punish disobedience. Sinners are justly charged as voluntary agents of their own ruin, provoking God of their own accord and not under compulsion; and it remains equally true that aiming at good is a special gift.

The last verse changes key, and Delitzsch hears the change as music. The longer form of the opening exclamation is a drawn-out sigh belonging to lament, the shorter to scornful complaint; from that note everything follows, soft and monotonous and slow, the lengthened word-forms themselves suiting elegy. Ellicott hears the same keynote and traces the harlot figure to the marriage by which Israel was won, made sharper because prostitution belonged to the actual ritual of the idolatries on offer; and he sharpens the last word, not casual homicide but assassins who have taken murder and robbery as a trade. Henry sets out what is lost, a city faithful to God and the public interest, justice administered on its thrones and righteousness resident in its palaces rather than called in to serve a turn. Wesley notes that one gross kind of wrong is made to stand for all.
22:
The two figures are read as one indictment of the rulers. Delitzsch makes the silver the princes and lords, the metal standing for nobility of character as well as birth, since refined silver reflects light in all its purity; what they had was the cluster of virtues the Latins gathered under one name, magnanimity and fairness and a mind above bribes, and what is left is the base stuff thrown off in refining. Ellicott says the same in economic terms: the coinage of judgment debased, the wine of enthusiasm watered till it strengthens nobody. Calvin keeps to appearances: the outward frame is not overturned, but dross looks like silver and thinned wine keeps its colour, so only taste betrays it.

Clarke defends the second figure against an objection nobody has made. Watering wine seems a weak image until one learns that in the Levant it is not done: a traveller reports Persians and Turks taking their wine neat and drinking water separately when they want the strength abated, and the Turks laughing at Christians for mixing. He notes the reversal, since among Greeks and Latins mixed wine always meant diluted. The adulteration is therefore not a household habit but a fraud.

Then the princes without a figure. Delitzsch hears the pun and finds two charges in it, rebellion towards God and partnership with thieves towards men, taking bribes of stolen goods and judging against the robbed; and not a few of them but every individual of that rank. Ellicott puts it as a report on provincial police under a modern government: the judge in secret partnership with the brigands, nothing moving without a payment, the men holding the plunder always able to outbid the man they took it from; and he finds irony in the word for bribes, which sounds like peace-offerings given instead of peace. Calvin locates the source, not the symptom, no disease being more injurious than one spreading from the head through the body, and quotes the proverb that servants are what the mistress is. Wesley adds that connivance makes a man a thief's companion as surely as violence does.

The sentence is introduced by a crowd of names. Delitzsch observes that nowhere else in the book are so many titles heaped together, three sealing an irrevocable decree with the thought of irresistible power. Ellicott notes the verb for saying is properly a whisper and always marks a solemn oracle, and that one name occurs in only a handful of places anywhere. Clarke stops at the strangeness of God easing himself: anger from an affront is painful and revenge removes it; and he names the figure, the ascribing to God of human sentiments and faculties, which Scripture uses with the utmost liberty.

The hand that moves is the chapter's turn. Delitzsch explains that God's hand rests while he leaves a man alone, and bringing it over someone usually means punishment and seldom rescue; here both, punishment as means and salvation as end. Ellicott compares the double face of the English word visit and thinks the context inclines to mercy. Gill will have only mercy, the hand of efficacious grace that plucks brands from the burning. Clarke pictures the workman, striking the scum off molten metal before it is poured, and remarks that he has watched it done with the naked hand and no harm taken. On the cleansing agent Clarke rejects soap, which has nothing to do with metals, and prefers a conjecture giving a furnace; Ellicott reads lye or potash, used in smelting, and guesses the prophet learned metallurgy from Phoenicians who fetched lead and tin from Spain. As for the restored judges, Ellicott looks back to David or the young Solomon as an Englishman looks back to Elizabeth; Gill and Clarke look forward to the Messiah; Calvin only remembers that a throne once mirrored a father's love.
27:
Whose righteousness redeems the city is the sharpest question left. Ellicott renders the preposition through rather than with and puts the condition in the verse before: redemption proceeds from God's compassion, but is impossible without the renewed justice of man to man, since that is of its essence. Calvin denies exactly this. It is a great mistake, he says, to refer the judgment and righteousness to the church, as though the prophet described a well-ordered city; God's own justice redeems her though men lend no help, and so the godly may keep hope while seeing nothing but obstructions. Delitzsch takes a third road: the words are God's right fulfilling itself judicially, so the judgment falling on sin frees what remained faithful. Clarke states a double operation, strict justice destroying the obdurate and faithfulness delivering the penitent.

The other half is for those who will not be redeemed. Delitzsch sorts the three terms: those broken away inwardly and outwardly, those living in open sin, those estranged by either road. Calvin uses the verse against a habit rather than a class: hypocrites have always been mingled with the church and judge it by outward show, so whatever God promises they apply at once to themselves; and he draws a rule for teachers: terrify the wicked without discouraging the good, comfort the good without letting the wicked pocket a promise.

Then the groves. Clarke describes them as a very ancient appendage of idolatry, each with its temple, altars and images and all the rites required, many of them impure; they were a principal part of the religion of Canaan, and the Israelites, commanded to destroy them, afterwards took to them themselves. Ellicott corrects the tree to the terebinth and reaches for Greek parallels, the groves of Daphne at Antioch and of Dodona, and that of the Eumenides at Colonos; the gardens he takes for the planted precinct round the central tree. Delitzsch blocks the reading that makes both mere objects of luxury, since the prophets use these words repeatedly for unlawful places of worship, and the verbs here are those used of choosing a false god.

The judgment fits the crime exactly. Delitzsch notes the terebinth is otherwise always green, so withered leaves mean prosperity destroyed, and a garden without water means the sources of help dried up; both, in that state, need only a spark. Clarke explains why a waterless garden is a ruin and not an inconvenience: there a garden left a few days without water is burnt up entirely, so every one draws on a river or a reservoir filled in season. Calvin turns the figure on his own century, where men light lamps and adorn temples, dazzle with gold, play organs and ring bells, and reckon themselves happiest of men, as if God had been paid a hundredfold and no evil could come from him.

The last verse burns, and they cannot agree who is in the fire. Wesley makes the strong one the idol its owners thought able to defend them, the maker one who can save neither himself nor his work. Calvin sharpens the word into address: that god who was your strength shall be turned into stubble. He reports the reading that finds repentant idolaters burning their images, and prefers his own, men and idols heaped like a woodpile so one conflagration takes both, the idols for tow and the men for fire. Delitzsch will not have the participle, since maker is a strange epithet for an idol and the figure would run backwards, the thing made kindling the man who made it; with the versions he reads his work. Ellicott follows and states the moral flatly, the sin itself becoming the instrument of destruction, and notes that tow and spark are the quickest combustion there is. Gill alone looks past them to a beast cast alive into a lake of fire.
